I'm working with some hierarchical data where each item has an associated 'emission' value. Items can have parent items, and there's also a percentage value indicating how much an item contributes to its parent's total.

My goal is to calculate a 'cumulative emission' for each item. For items at the bottom of the hierarchy (those without children), this cumulative value is simply their own emission value. For items that are parents, their cumulative value should be their own emission plus a portion of their direct children's cumulative emissions, weighted by that percentage contribution value associated with each child. The challenge is that a child's total value also depends on *its* children, and so on down the hierarchy.

I've tried different approaches to walk through the hierarchy and sum these values up, but I'm having trouble getting the calculation right, especially when it comes to applying the percentage contributions correctly as the values accumulate up the tree. The final totals I'm getting don't seem correct.

How can I structure a query in PostgreSQL to correctly calculate this cumulative emission for every item in the hierarchy, considering both its own emission and the properly weighted contributions rolling up from all its descendants? I need the final output to show the item's ID, its parent's ID, and this final calculated cumulative total value.
issue_sql:
WITH RECURSIVE HierarchyCTE(entityid, parentid, emission, total_emission, percentage, level) AS (
    SELECT entityid, parentid, emission, emission AS total_emission, pctcontribution, 0
    FROM tree_table
    WHERE NOT entityid IN (SELECT DISTINCT parentid FROM tree_table WHERE NOT parentid IS NULL)
    UNION ALL
    SELECT h.entityid, h.parentid, h.emission, h.emission + cte.total_emission * (CAST(cte.pctcontribution AS DOUBLE PRECISION) / NULLIF(100, 0)) AS total_emission, h.pctcontribution, cte.level + 1
    FROM tree_table AS h
    JOIN hierarchycte AS cte ON h.entityid = cte.parentid
)
SELECT entityid, parentid, SUM(total_emission) AS total_emission
FROM (
    SELECT entityid, parentid, SUM(total_emission) AS total_emission, level
    FROM hierarchycte
    GROUP BY entityid, parentid, level
)
GROUP BY entityid, parentid
ORDER BY entityid NULLS FIRST
sol_sql:
WITH RECURSIVE cte(root, entityid, parentid, entity_emission, pctcontribution) AS (
    SELECT entityid, entityid, COALESCE(parentid, entityid), emission, pctcontribution
    FROM tree_table
    WHERE parentid IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT cte.root, t.entityid, t.parentid, t.emission, t.pctcontribution
    FROM cte
    INNER JOIN tree_table AS t ON (t.parentid = cte.entityid)
),
grid AS (
    SELECT
        x.root,
        x.entityid,
        x.parentid,
        x.entity_emission,
        x.groupid,
        x.cumulative_total,
        x.pctcontribution,
        CASE
            WHEN x.entityid = x.root THEN 0
            WHEN x.entityid <> x.root AND x.entityid <> x.groupid AND x.groupid = x.root THEN
                CAST(x.entity_emission * (100 - x.pctcontribution) AS DOUBLE PRECISION) / NULLIF(100, 0)
            WHEN x.entityid <> x.root AND x.entityid = x.groupid THEN
                CAST(LAG(x.entity_emission * (100 - x.pctcontribution)) OVER (PARTITION BY x.root, x.groupid ORDER BY x.entityid NULLS FIRST) AS DOUBLE PRECISION) / NULLIF(100, 0)
            ELSE 0
        END AS contribution_correction
    FROM (
        SELECT
            root,
            entityid,
            parentid,
            entity_emission,
            COALESCE(LAG(parentid) OVER (ORDER BY root NULLS FIRST, parentid NULLS FIRST, entityid NULLS FIRST), parentid) AS groupid,
            CAST(
                CASE
                    WHEN entityid = root THEN SUM(entity_emission) OVER (PARTITION BY root)
                    ELSE
                        CASE
                            WHEN COALESCE(LAG(parentid) OVER (ORDER BY entityid NULLS FIRST), parentid) = parentid THEN entity_emission
                            ELSE SUM(entity_emission) OVER (PARTITION BY root ORDER BY entityid NULLS FIRST)
                        END
                END
            AS NUMERIC) AS cumulative_total,
            pctcontribution
        FROM cte
        ORDER BY entityid NULLS FIRST
    ) AS x
)
SELECT
    g.entityid,
    g.parentid,
    CAST(
        CASE
            WHEN g.entityid = g.root THEN
                (SUM(CASE WHEN g.entityid <> g.root THEN g.corrected_contribution ELSE 0 END) OVER (PARTITION BY g.root) +
                (MAX(CASE WHEN g.entityid = g.root THEN g.entity_emission ELSE 0 END) OVER (PARTITION BY g.root)) -
                SUM(g.group_correction) OVER (PARTITION BY g.root))
            WHEN g.entityid <> g.root AND g.entityid <> g.groupid AND g.groupid = g.root THEN g.entity_emission
            WHEN g.entityid <> g.root AND g.entityid <> g.groupid THEN g.entity_emission
            WHEN g.entityid <> g.root AND g.entityid = g.groupid THEN g.corrected_contribution
            ELSE 0
        END
    AS NUMERIC) AS cumulative_contribution_total
FROM (
    SELECT
        g.root,
        g.entityid,
        g.parentid,
        g.entity_emission,
        g.groupid,
        g.cumulative_total,
        g.pctcontribution,
        CAST(
            CASE
                WHEN g.entityid = g.root THEN SUM(g.entity_emission - g.contribution_correction) OVER (PARTITION BY g.root)
                WHEN g.entityid <> g.root AND g.entityid <> g.groupid AND g.groupid = g.root THEN g.cumulative_total - g.contribution_correction
                WHEN g.entityid <> g.root AND g.entityid = g.groupid THEN g.cumulative_total - g.contribution_correction
                ELSE 0
            END
        AS NUMERIC) AS corrected_contribution,
        CASE
            WHEN g.entityid <> g.root AND g.entityid = g.groupid THEN
                MAX(CASE
                    WHEN g.entityid <> g.root AND g.entityid = g.groupid THEN
                        CAST((g.cumulative_total - g.contribution_correction) * (100 - g.pctcontribution) AS DOUBLE PRECISION) / NULLIF(100, 0)
                    ELSE 0
                END) OVER (PARTITION BY g.root, g.groupid)
            ELSE 0
        END AS group_correction
    FROM grid AS g
    ORDER BY g.root NULLS FIRST, g.groupid NULLS FIRST, g.entityid NULLS FIRST
) AS g

First, the procedure needs to determine the total number of rows already present in the target table. Second, it needs to find the next available identifier, presumably by finding the maximum current identifier and adding one.

It seems like the inserts aren't using the values correctly, perhaps because of how I'm referencing the variables within the insert logic, or maybe there's an issue with how I'm calculating the initial values. I'm particularly unsure if using variable names that might be the same as column names could be causing problems inside the loop's insert statement.

How can I reliably write a PL/pgSQL procedure to first calculate the current row count and the next sequential ID from a table, and then use these values within a loop to insert the correct number of new rows back into that same table?

How can I structure a query in PostgreSQL to calculate this count of overlapping durations for every distinct time interval defined by the created_date and modified_date points in my tables?

WITH track_playlists AS (
    SELECT t.track_id, t.album_id, t.name,
           STRING_AGG(pt.playlist_id::text, ',' ORDER BY pt.playlist_id::text NULLS FIRST) AS connected_playlists
    FROM track AS t
    LEFT JOIN playlist_track AS pt ON t.track_id = pt.track_id
    GROUP BY t.track_id, t.album_id, t.name
),
album_stats AS (
    SELECT a.album_id, ar.name AS artist_name,
           COUNT(t.track_id) OVER (PARTITION BY a.album_id) AS track_count,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY a.album_id ORDER BY a.album_id NULLS FIRST) AS rn

    LEFT JOIN artist AS ar ON a.artist_id = ar.artist_id

       p.name

My goal is to produce a result set containing an ID (which could be either a track's ID or an album's ID), the associated album identifier, and a third column representing a specific value. This value column should ideally contain the name for a track record. However, if the record represents an album, or if the name information isn't available for a track, it should display the media type name instead.

I've attempted to combine the track and album information based on their shared album identifier using joins. I've also tried using some conditional logic to make sure the track name takes precedence over the media type name in my value column. But I'm running into issues getting this combined view right – sometimes I seem to be missing entries, or the value column doesn't correctly reflect the track name/media type prioritization. My attempts feel more complex than they should be for this task.

query:
I'm working with a dataset of invoices, each having a date. My goal is to see how the frequency of invoices has changed over time. Specifically, for every distinct customer, I want to calculate the difference between the number of invoices in their most recent year of activity and the number of invoices in their earliest year of activity.

I've tried grouping the invoices by customer and then attempting to count occurrences based on the overall earliest and latest years in the entire dataset. However, this doesn't seem right because some customers might not have invoices in the absolute earliest or latest year recorded across all invoices. The results I'm getting don't seem to reflect the change *within* each customer's own timeline.

How can I correctly calculate this difference for each customer, ensuring I'm comparing the count from the very last year that specific customer had an invoice with the count from the very first year that same customer had an invoice?
issue_sql:
SELECT
    TO_CHAR(customer_id) AS customer,
    COUNT(CASE WHEN EXTRACT(YEAR FROM invoice_date) = recent_year THEN 1 END) -
    COUNT(CASE WHEN EXTRACT(YEAR FROM invoice_date) = oldest_year THEN 1 END) AS year_difference
FROM invoice,
    (
        SELECT
            MAX(EXTRACT(YEAR FROM invoice_date)) AS recent_year,
            MIN(EXTRACT(YEAR FROM invoice_date)) AS oldest_year
        FROM invoice
    ) year_range
GROUP BY TO_CHAR(customer_id), recent_year, oldest_year;
sol_sql:
SELECT customer_id,
    (SELECT COUNT(*)
     FROM invoice e2
     WHERE e2.customer_id = e1.customer_id
     AND EXTRACT(YEAR FROM e2.invoice_date) =
         (SELECT MAX(EXTRACT(YEAR FROM invoice_date))
          FROM invoice e3
          WHERE e3.customer_id = e1.customer_id)
    ) -
    (SELECT COUNT(*)
     FROM invoice e2
     WHERE e2.customer_id = e1.customer_id
     AND EXTRACT(YEAR FROM e2.invoice_date) =
         (SELECT MIN(EXTRACT(YEAR FROM invoice_date))
          FROM invoice e3
          WHERE e3.customer_id = e1.customer_id)
    ) AS e
FROM invoice e1
GROUP BY customer_id

Specifically, for every distinct employee title, I want to calculate the difference between the number of times that employee title occurred in its most recent year of activity and the number of times it occurred in its earliest year of activity.
I've tried grouping the employees by title and then attempting to count occurrences based on the overall earliest and latest years in the entire dataset.     TO_CHAR(title) AS employee_title,
    COUNT(CASE WHEN EXTRACT(YEAR FROM from_date) = recent_year THEN 1 END) -
    COUNT(CASE WHEN EXTRACT(YEAR FROM from_date) = oldest_year THEN 1 END) AS year_difference
FROM title,
    (
        SELECT
            MAX(EXTRACT(YEAR FROM from_date)) AS recent_year,
            MIN(EXTRACT(YEAR FROM from_date)) AS oldest_year
        FROM title
    ) year_range
GROUP BY TO_CHAR(title), recent_year, oldest_year;

     FROM title e2
     WHERE e2.title = e1.title

          FROM title e3
          WHERE e3.title = e1.title)
    ) -
    (SELECT COUNT(*)
     FROM title e2
     WHERE e2.title = e1.title
     AND EXTRACT(YEAR FROM e2.from_date) =
         (SELECT MIN(EXTRACT(YEAR FROM from_date))
          FROM title e3
          WHERE e3.title = e1.title)
    ) AS e
FROM title e1

I'm working with data about tracks and other tables in the Chinook database. I've processed this data to create two distinct sets of track information, let's call them set A and set B, each containing tracks ranked based on certain properties. My goal is to compare these two sets to find out how many tracks appear identically in both (based on their ID and rank), how many are unique to set A after filtering, and how many are unique to set B after filtering.

The comparison gets complicated because I need to apply several filters. One filter, in particular, is causing trouble: I need to ensure that tracks considered from set A are associated with a very specific genre, identified by a value like `1`. When I try to apply this filter condition directly in my comparison logic, my query doesn't work as expected. It seems this check might be identifying multiple genres for a single track when the logic expects a single value for comparison, leading to errors or incorrect counts. I've tried different ways to incorporate this check alongside other conditions (like ensuring certain related albums have the same artist), but I'm struggling to get the final counts right.

How can I structure a query to effectively compare these two derived sets and get the three counts (common items, items only in A, items only in B), while correctly handling complex filtering logic, especially the condition related to the specific genre `1`, without running into errors caused by potentially multiple matching genres?
issue_sql:
WITH

    set_a (track_id, genre_count) AS (
        SELECT track_id, COUNT(DISTINCT genre_id)
        FROM track
        GROUP BY track_id
        HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT genre_id) > 1
    ),
    set_b (track_id, genre_count) AS (
        SELECT a.track_id, COUNT(DISTINCT b.genre_id)
        FROM track a
        JOIN genre b ON a.genre_id = b.genre_id
        WHERE b.name IS NOT NULL
        GROUP BY a.track_id
    ),

    unique_a (track_id, genre_count, rn, density_rank) AS (
        SELECT
            track_id,
            genre_count,
            ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY track_id ORDER BY genre_count) AS rn,
            DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY genre_count DESC) AS density_rank
        FROM set_a
    ),
    unique_b (track_id, genre_count, rn, density_rank) AS (
        SELECT
            track_id,
            genre_count,
            ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY track_id ORDER BY genre_count) AS rn,
            DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY genre_count DESC) AS density_rank
        FROM set_b
    ),

    track_hierarchy AS (
        SELECT
            track_id,
            track_id AS root_track,
            1 AS hierarchy_level
        FROM track
        WHERE genre_id = 1

        UNION ALL

        SELECT
            m.track_id,
            h.root_track,
            h.hierarchy_level + 1
        FROM track m
        JOIN track_hierarchy h ON m.track_id = h.track_id
    )
SELECT
    COUNT(CASE WHEN a.rn = b.rn AND a.density_rank = b.density_rank THEN 1 END) AS num_identical_in_a_and_b,
    COUNT(CASE WHEN a.track_id IS NULL THEN 1 END) AS num_not_identical_in_a,
    COUNT(CASE WHEN b.track_id IS NULL THEN 1 END) AS num_not_identical_in_b,
    STRING_AGG(CAST(a.track_id AS VARCHAR), ',') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY a.density_rank) AS matching_tracks,
    JSON_AGG(
        JSON_BUILD_OBJECT(
            'track', a.track_id,
            'rank', a.density_rank
        )
        ORDER BY b.density_rank
    ) AS track_json
FROM unique_a a
FULL OUTER JOIN unique_b b ON a.track_id = b.track_id AND a.rn = b.rn
LEFT JOIN track_hierarchy h ON a.track_id = h.track_id
WHERE

    (SELECT genre_id
     FROM track
     WHERE track.track_id = a.track_id) = 1

    AND EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM track c
        JOIN album a1 ON c.album_id = a1.album_id
        JOIN artist a2 ON a1.artist_id = a2.artist_id
        WHERE c.track_id = a.track_id
        AND a1.artist_id = a2.artist_id
    )
GROUP BY
    GROUPING SETS (
        (a.density_rank, b.density_rank),
        ()
    )
HAVING
    COUNT(DISTINCT a.track_id) > (
        SELECT AVG(genre_count)
        FROM set_a
    )

    x) AS (
    SELECT 1
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 2
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 1
),

set_b (
    x) AS (
    SELECT 1
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 2
),

unique_a (x, rn) AS (
    SELECT
        x,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY x
            ORDER BY (SELECT NULL)
        ) AS rn
    FROM set_a
),

unique_b (x, rn) AS (
    SELECT
        x,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY x
            ORDER BY (SELECT NULL)
        ) AS rn
    FROM set_b
)

SELECT
    COUNT(CASE
        WHEN a.rn = b.rn THEN 1
    END) AS num_identical_in_a_and_b,
    COUNT(CASE
        WHEN a.rn IS NULL THEN 1
    END) AS num_not_identical_in_a,

        WHEN b.rn IS NULL THEN 1
    END) AS num_not_identical_in_b
FROM unique_a a
FULL OUTER JOIN unique_b

query: I'm working with a dataset and I'm trying to identify consecutive winning streaks. My goal is to get a list showing each team, the start date of a winning streak, the end date of that streak, and how many games were won consecutively during that period.
issue_sql:
SELECT "inventory_id" AS "team_api_id",
       "start_date",
       "end_date",
       "match_count"
FROM "lego_inventory_parts" MATCH_RECOGNIZE (PARTITION BY "color_id"
                              ORDER BY "part_num" MEASURES FIRST("part_num") AS "start_date", LAST("part_num") AS "end_date", COUNT(*) AS "match_count" PATTERN (consecutive_wins+) DEFINE consecutive_wins AS "part_num" = 'EUROPEAN_FOOTBALL_2')
sol_sql:
WITH home_wins AS (
  SELECT
    inventory_id,
    part_num,
    CASE WHEN quantity > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_win,
    CASE WHEN quantity > 0 THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS is_not_win
  FROM lego_inventory_parts
),
win_groups AS (
  SELECT
    inventory_id,
    part_num,
    is_win,
    SUM(is_not_win) OVER (PARTITION BY inventory_id ORDER BY part_num) AS win_group
  FROM home_wins
  WHERE is_win = 1
),
win_streaks AS (
  SELECT
    inventory_id,
    win_group,
    MIN(part_num) AS start_date,
    MAX(part_num) AS end_date,
    COUNT(*) AS match_count
  FROM win_groups
  GROUP BY inventory_id, win_group
)
SELECT
  inventory_id AS team_api_id,
  start_date,
  end_date,
  match_count
FROM win_streaks
ORDER BY team_api_id, start_date;

I'm trying to query my track data, which is associated with different albums. For each distinct album, I only want to retrieve the first two associated tracks, based on the track's ID order.

I've attempted to rank or number the tracks within each album group and then filter based on that rank. However, I'm finding it tricky to get just those top two rows per album correctly. My attempts either seem to return all tracks or don't quite isolate the first two as intended.

How can I structure a query in PostgreSQL to select only the first two tracks for each album, ordered by their respective track IDs?
issue_sql:
WITH track_stats AS (
    SELECT
        album_id,
        COUNT(*) AS track_count,
        (array_agg(name ORDER BY track_id))[1] AS first_name,
        (array_agg(name ORDER BY track_id DESC))[1] AS last_name
    FROM "track"
    GROUP BY album_id
),
ranked_tracks AS (
    SELECT
        a."track_id",
        a."album_id",
        a."name",
        DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY a."album_id" ORDER BY a."track_id") AS track_rank,
        stats.track_count,
        stats.first_name,
        stats.last_name
    FROM "track" a
    JOIN track_stats stats ON a."album_id" = stats.album_id
),
filtered_tracks AS (
    SELECT
        ra.*,
        CASE
            WHEN ra.track_rank <= 2 THEN 'TOP'
            WHEN ra.track_rank > ra.track_count - 2 THEN 'BOTTOM'
            ELSE 'MIDDLE'
        END AS position,
        LAG(ra."name") OVER (PARTITION BY ra."album_id" ORDER BY ra."track_id") AS prev_name,
        LEAD(ra."name") OVER (PARTITION BY ra."album_id" ORDER BY ra."track_id") AS next_name
    FROM ranked_tracks ra
)
SELECT
    fa."track_id",
    fa."album_id",
    fa."name",
    fa.track_rank AS rnk,
    fa.position,
    fa.prev_name,
    fa.next_name,
    fa.first_name,
    fa.last_name
FROM filtered_tracks fa
WHERE fa.track_rank <= 2
GROUP BY
    fa."track_id",
    fa."album_id",
    fa."name",
    fa.track_rank,
    fa.position,
    fa.prev_name,
    fa.next_name,
    fa.first_name,
    fa.last_name
ORDER BY fa."album_id", fa.track_rank
sol_sql:
SELECT *
FROM
    (SELECT
        a.*,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY a.album_id
            ORDER BY a.track_id
        ) AS rnk
    FROM track a) subquery
WHERE rnk <= 2

issue_sql:
WITH RECURSIVE movie_hierarchy AS (

    SELECT
        m.id,
        m.title,
        m.id AS root_movie_id,
        1 AS hierarchy_level,
        '/' || m.id AS movie_path
    FROM movie m
    WHERE m.id > 0

    UNION ALL

    SELECT
        m.id,
        m.title,
        h.root_movie_id,
        h.hierarchy_level + 1,
        h.movie_path || '/' || m.id
    FROM movie_hierarchy h
    JOIN movie m ON h.id != m.id
    WHERE h.id != m.id
),
month_generator AS (

    SELECT
        TO_DATE('01/01/2018', 'MM/DD/YYYY') AS month_start_date,
        1 AS month_num

    UNION ALL

    SELECT
        month_start_date + INTERVAL '1 month',
        month_num + 1
    FROM month_generator
    WHERE month_num < 12
),
movie_months AS (

    SELECT
        mg.month_start_date,
        mh.id,
        mh.title,
        mh.hierarchy_level,
        mh.movie_path
    FROM month_generator mg
    CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
        SELECT
            h.id,
            h.title,
            h.hierarchy_level,
            h.movie_path
        FROM movie_hierarchy h
        WHERE h.hierarchy_level <= mg.month_num
    ) mh
)
SELECT
    mm.month_start_date,
    mm.id,
    mm.title,
    mm.hierarchy_level,
    mm.movie_path
FROM movie_months mm
WHERE mm.month_start_date BETWEEN TO_DATE('01/01/2018', 'MM/DD/YYYY')
                              AND TO_DATE('12/31/2018', 'MM/DD/YYYY')
ORDER BY
    mm.month_start_date,
    mm.hierarchy_level,
    mm.id

    m.title

I'm working with some data in PostgreSQL where I need to pull specific credit values based on choices made. I have one set of data that links an ID to various credit amounts across different categories – think Art, Business, Nature, etc., all in separate columns for each ID. Then, I have another set of data recording which category each ID actually chose at different times.

My goal is to generate a list showing each ID, the category they chose, and the *specific* credit value associated with *that chosen category* for that ID. For example, if ID 5001 chose 'ART', I need the result row to show ID 5001, 'ART', and whatever the credit value is in the Art credit column for ID 5001. If the same ID also made a choice for 'BIZ', I'd expect another row showing that choice and the corresponding Business credit value.

I've tried joining these pieces of information and using conditional logic to figure out which credit column to pull from based on the choice made. However, I'm running into issues where the results don't seem right – I might be getting summed values or results that don't accurately reflect the single credit value for the specific choice. It feels like maybe I'm aggregating incorrectly or making the join more complex than it needs to be.

How can I structure my query in PostgreSQL to correctly link each ID's choice to the corresponding credit value from the correct category column, ensuring I get just that specific value for each choice record?

I'm trying to reshape some data I have in my PostgreSQL database. Currently, I have information stored vertically, meaning each row represents a specific characteristic for an employee, like their first name ('first_name'), last name ('last_name'), or birth date ('birth_date'), along with the employee's identifier.

What I need is to transform this data so that each employee has only one row, and their different characteristics ('first_name', 'last_name', 'birth_date') are presented in separate columns next to their identifier.

I've tried a few approaches to group the information by employee and then extract the specific values for each characteristic type into its own column, but I'm finding it tricky to get the structure right. My attempts haven't quite produced the clean, single-row-per-employee output I'm looking for, and it feels like I might be overcomplicating things.

For example, if I have rows like ('10001', 'first_name', 'Georgi'), ('10001', 'last_name', 'Facello'), ('10001', 'birth_date', '1953-09-02'), ('10002', 'first_name', 'Bezalel'), etc., I want the final result to look like:

10001 | Georgi | Facello | 1953-09-02
10002 | Bezalel | Simmel | 1964-06-02

How can I effectively pivot this row-based characteristic data into distinct columns for each employee in PostgreSQL?

WITH employee_data AS (
    SELECT
        e.id AS employee_id,
        'first_name' AS attribute_type,
        e.first_name AS attribute_value
    FROM employee e
    WHERE e.id IS NOT NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT
        e.id AS employee_id,
        'last_name' AS attribute_type,
        e.last_name AS attribute_value
    FROM employee e
    WHERE e.id IS NOT NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT
        e.id AS employee_id,
        'birth_date' AS attribute_type,
        CAST(e.birth_date AS TEXT) AS attribute_value
    FROM employee e
    WHERE e.id IS NOT NULL
),
employee_stats AS (
    SELECT
        employee_id,
        attribute_type,
        attribute_value,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY employee_id, attribute_type ORDER BY attribute_value) AS rn
    FROM employee_data
)
SELECT
    employee_id,
    (xpath('//attr[@type="first_name"]/text()',
        xmlagg(
            xmlelement(name attr,
                xmlattributes(attribute_type AS type),
                attribute_value
            )
            ORDER BY attribute_type
        )
    ))[1]::text AS first_name,
    (xpath('//attr[@type="last_name"]/text()',
        xmlagg(
            xmlelement(name attr,
                xmlattributes(attribute_type AS type),
                attribute_value
            )
            ORDER BY attribute_type
        )
    ))[1]::text AS last_name,
    (xpath('//attr[@type="birth_date"]/text()',
        xmlagg(
            xmlelement(name attr,
                xmlattributes(attribute_type AS type),

            ORDER BY attribute_type

FROM employee_stats

            xmlagg(
                xmlelement(name attr,
                    xmlattributes(attribute_type AS type),
                    attribute_value
                )
            )
        ))[1]::text IS NULL THEN '0'
        ELSE (xpath('//attr[@type="birth_date"]/text()',
            xmlagg(

                    attribute_value

            )
        ))[1]::text
    END

WITH employee_data AS (
  SELECT
    e.employee_id AS "pk",
    CASE
      WHEN e.employee_id % 2 = 0 THEN 'Even'
      ELSE 'Odd'

    SUBSTRING(e.city FROM 1 FOR POSITION(' ' IN e.city) - 1) AS "col3",
    TO_TIMESTAMP(TO_CHAR(e.hire_date, 'YYYY/MM/DD') || ' ' ||
           LPAD(CAST(MOD(ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY e.employee_id), 24) AS TEXT), 2, '0') || ':' ||
           LPAD(CAST(MOD(ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY e.employee_id) * 7, 60) AS TEXT), 2, '0'),

  SELECT
    ed."pk",

    ed."col3",

issue_sql:
WITH columns (column_name) AS
  (SELECT 'album_id'
   UNION ALL SELECT 'name'
   UNION ALL SELECT 'composer'),
     column_exists (column_name,
                      column_exists) AS
  (SELECT c.column_name,
          COALESCE(a.attname, 'NO')
   FROM columns c
   LEFT OUTER JOIN pg_attribute a ON (a.attrelid = 'track'::regclass
                                      AND c.column_name = a.attname))
SELECT *
FROM column_exists
PIVOT (MAX(column_exists)
       FOR column_name IN ('album_id', 'name', 'composer'))
WHERE
    (SELECT column_name
     FROM columns) = 'album_id';

    SELECT 'album_id' AS column_name
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'name'
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'composer'
),

column_exists AS (
    SELECT
        c.column_name,
        CASE WHEN a.column_name IS NOT NULL THEN 'YES' ELSE 'NO' END AS column_exists
    FROM columns c
    LEFT OUTER JOIN information_schema.columns a
        ON (
            a.table_name = 'track'
            AND c.column_name = a.column_name
            AND a.table_schema = current_schema()

)

My goal is to get a result that clearly shows whether each of these columns is present, ideally in a single row format where each column name corresponds to one of the columns I'm checking, and the value indicates if it exists (like 'YES' or 'NO').

I've looked into querying system information tables to get column details, which seems promising for finding out if a column exists individually. However, I'm running into trouble when trying to consolidate this information into the specific single-row output I need. Instead of getting one summary row, my attempts often result in multiple rows, one for each column I check, or I just can't figure out how to transform the existence check results into separate columns in one row.

How can I structure a query to check for the presence of 'id', 'name', and 'rgb' in my table and display the outcome as a single row with columns like `id`, `name`, and `rgb`, showing 'YES' or 'NO' for each based on whether they exist?
issue_sql:
WITH columns (column_name) AS (
  SELECT 'id'
   UNION ALL SELECT 'name'
   UNION ALL SELECT 'rgb'
),
column_exists (column_name, column_exists) AS (
  SELECT c.column_name,
          COALESCE(a.attname, 'NO')
   FROM columns c
   LEFT OUTER JOIN pg_attribute a ON (a.attrelid = 'lego_colors'::regclass
                                      AND c.column_name = a.attname)
)
SELECT *
FROM column_exists
PIVOT (MAX(column_exists)
       FOR column_name IN ('id', 'name', 'rgb'))
WHERE
    (SELECT column_name
     FROM columns) = 'id';
sol_sql:
WITH columns AS (
    SELECT 'id' AS column_name
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'name'
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'rgb'
),

column_exists AS (
    SELECT
        c.column_name,
        CASE WHEN a.column_name IS NOT NULL THEN 'YES' ELSE 'NO' END AS column_exists
    FROM columns c
    LEFT OUTER JOIN information_schema.columns a
        ON (
            a.table_name = 'lego_colors'
            AND c.column_name = a.column_name
            AND a.table_schema = current_schema()
        )
)

SELECT
    MAX(CASE WHEN column_name = 'id' THEN column_exists END) AS id,
    MAX(CASE WHEN column_name = 'name' THEN column_exists END) AS name,
    MAX(CASE WHEN column_name = 'rgb' THEN column_exists END) AS rgb
FROM column_exists;

def test_case(pred_sqls, sol_sqls, db_name, conn):
    pred_sqls = remove_distinct(pred_sqls)
    sol_sqls = remove_distinct(sol_sqls)
    result = ex_base(pred_sqls, sol_sqls, db_name, conn)
    assert result == 1, f"ex_base returned {result} but expected 1."
    return result

query:
I'm trying to compare two comma-separated strings in PostgreSQL to find the values they share. For instance, I have one string '24,36,78,98' and another '25,36,88,98'.

My goal is to get a result containing only the numbers that appear in both strings. For the example strings, the expected output would be the values '36' and '98'.

I've attempted to split the strings into individual numbers and then compare them, but I'm having trouble getting just the common elements correctly. It seems more complicated than I initially thought.

How can I effectively compare these two strings in PostgreSQL to extract only the values they have in common?
issue_sql:
WITH string1_tab AS (
    SELECT REGEXP_SUBSTR('24,36,78,98', '[^,]+', 1, generate_series) AS value,
           generate_series AS position
    FROM generate_series(1, LENGTH('24,36,78,98') - LENGTH(REPLACE('24,36,78,98', ',', '')) + 1)
),
string2_tab AS (
    SELECT REGEXP_SUBSTR('25,36,88,98', '[^,]+', 1, generate_series) AS value,
           generate_series AS position
    FROM generate_series(1, LENGTH('25,36,88,98') - LENGTH(REPLACE('25,36,88,98', ',', '')) + 1)
),
string1_parsed AS (
    SELECT TO_NUMBER(TRIM(value), '999999') AS num_value
    FROM string1_tab
),
string2_parsed AS (
    SELECT TO_NUMBER(TRIM(value), '999999') AS num_value
    FROM string2_tab
),
common_values AS (
    SELECT s1.num_value
    FROM string1_parsed s1
    JOIN string2_parsed s2 ON s1.num_value = s2.num_value
)
SELECT STRING_AGG(num_value::text, ',') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY num_value) AS common_values
FROM common_values
WHERE num_value IS NOT NULL
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT num_value) > 0
sol_sql:
WITH string1_tab AS (
    SELECT unnest(string_to_array('24,36,78,98', ',')) AS value
),
string2_tab AS (
    SELECT unnest(string_to_array('25,36,88,98', ',')) AS value
)
SELECT *
FROM string1_tab
INTERSECT
SELECT *
FROM string2_tab

    result = ex_base(pred_sqls, sol_sqls, db_name, conn)
    assert result == 1, f"ex_base returned {result} but expected 1."

query:
I'm working with some invoice data where the invoice date is stored as a timestamp. My goal is to calculate the difference in days between each invoice date and the current date.

Furthermore, I need to calculate a flag ('Y' or 'N') for each invoice based on some conditions derived using window functions. Specifically, I need to look at groups of invoices based on their date (ignoring the time part) and a specific identifier. Within each group, I need to find the minimum duration (days from invoice date to current date) and also count how many records share the exact same date, identifier, and calculated duration.

The flag should be 'Y' if either the minimum duration calculated for that date/identifier group is zero, OR if the count calculated for that specific record's date/identifier/duration combination is greater than one. Otherwise, the flag should be 'N'.

I've been trying to structure this using window functions, but I'm running into difficulties getting the calculations for the minimum duration and the counts within the partitions correct. I'm not getting the results I expect for the flag.

How can I correctly calculate the duration from the invoice date field to the current date, and then use window functions effectively in PostgreSQL to determine the minimum duration and counts required for my conditional flag logic?
issue_sql:
WITH t AS
  (SELECT invoice_date,
          invoice_id AS code,
          CURRENT_DATE - DATE(invoice_date) AS duration,
          COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY DATE(invoice_date), invoice_id, CURRENT_DATE - DATE(invoice_date)) AS cnt,
          MIN(CURRENT_DATE - DATE(invoice_date)) OVER (PARTITION BY DATE(invoice_date), invoice_id) AS min_dur
   FROM invoice)
SELECT t.invoice_date,
       t.code,
       t.duration,
       CASE
           WHEN t.min_dur = 0
                OR MAX(t.cnt) OVER (PARTITION BY t.invoice_date, t.code) > 1 THEN 'Y'
           ELSE 'N'
       END AS flg
FROM t
WHERE invoice_date = '2021-01-09 00:00:00'
sol_sql:
WITH t AS (
    SELECT
        invoice_date,
        invoice_id AS code,
        CURRENT_DATE - CAST(invoice_date AS DATE) AS duration,
        COUNT(*) OVER (
            PARTITION BY
                CAST(invoice_date AS DATE),
                invoice_id,
                CURRENT_DATE - CAST(invoice_date AS DATE)
        ) AS cnt,
        MIN(CURRENT_DATE - CAST(invoice_date AS DATE)) OVER (
            PARTITION BY
                CAST(invoice_date AS DATE),
                invoice_id
        ) AS min_dur
    FROM invoice
)

SELECT
    t.invoice_date,
    t.code,
    t.duration,
    CASE
        WHEN
            t.min_dur = 0
            OR MAX(t.cnt) OVER (PARTITION BY t.invoice_date, t.code) > 1 THEN 'Y'
        ELSE 'N'
    END AS flg
FROM t

    SELECT
        employee_id,
        from_date,
        amount,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY employee_id ORDER BY from_date DESC) as rn,
        AVG(amount) OVER () as overall_avg_salary

employee_details AS (
    SELECT
        e.id,
        e.first_name,
        e.last_name,
        s.amount as salary,
        ess.overall_avg_salary

    JOIN salary s ON e.id = s.employee_id

)

I'm trying to select track genres and their total price, but I need to apply a cumulative limit. I've managed to calculate the total price for each genre and have ordered these genres alphabetically in descending order (Z to A).

My goal is to get a list of these genres, starting from the top of my descending list, such that their combined price doesn't go over a specific threshold, say $800. The issue I'm running into is how to correctly stop accumulating once the threshold is about to be breached. When I tried calculating a cumulative sum and filtering, I sometimes end up including the genre that actually pushes the total *over* $800. What I really want is to include only the genres up to the point *before* the cumulative total exceeds $800.

So, starting with the genres sorted Z-A, I want to keep adding the price amounts until the total is less than or equal to $800. How can I structure a query in PostgreSQL to get this specific list of genres and their price totals, ensuring the cumulative sum respects the $800 cap and excludes the genre that would cause it to be exceeded?
issue_sql:
WITH OrderedCategories AS (
    SELECT
        SUM(unit_price) AS category_total,
        g.name as category
    FROM track t JOIN genre g ON t.genre_id = g.genre_id
    GROUP BY g.name
    ORDER BY g.name DESC
),
Cumulative AS (
    SELECT category_total, category,
           SUM(category_total) OVER (ORDER BY category DESC ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS cumulative_sum
    FROM OrderedCategories
)
SELECT category_total, category
FROM Cumulative
WHERE cumulative_sum <= 800
AND (cumulative_sum - category_total) < 800
sol_sql:
WITH RECURSIVE OrderedCategories AS (
  SELECT
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY g.name DESC) AS rn,
    g.name as category,
    SUM(unit_price) AS category_total
  FROM track t JOIN genre g ON t.genre_id = g.genre_id
  WHERE g.name IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY g.name
),
RecursiveCTE AS (
  SELECT
    rn,
    category,
    category_total,
    category_total AS cumulative_total,
    CASE
      WHEN category_total <= 800 THEN 1 ELSE 0
    END AS included
  FROM OrderedCategories
  WHERE rn = 1

  UNION ALL

  SELECT
    oc.rn,
    oc.category,
    oc.category_total,
    CASE
      WHEN r.cumulative_total + oc.category_total <= 800 THEN r.cumulative_total + oc.category_total
      ELSE r.cumulative_total
    END AS cumulative_total,
    CASE
      WHEN r.cumulative_total + oc.category_total <= 800 THEN 1 ELSE 0
    END AS included
  FROM RecursiveCTE r
  JOIN OrderedCategories oc ON oc.rn = r.rn + 1
)
SELECT category, category_total
FROM RecursiveCTE
WHERE included = 1
ORDER BY rn

    SELECT
        invoice_date,
        invoice_id,
        EXTRACT(HOUR FROM invoice_date) + EXTRACT(MINUTE FROM invoice_date)/60 AS hour_of_day,
        TO_CHAR(invoice_date, 'YYYY-MM-DD') AS invoice_date_str
    FROM invoice
),
target_times AS (
    SELECT 8 AS target_hour
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 20 AS target_hour
),
distance_calc AS (
    SELECT
        it.invoice_date,
        it.invoice_id,
        it.invoice_date_str,
        tt.target_hour,
        CASE
            WHEN tt.target_hour = 8 THEN 'morning'
            WHEN tt.target_hour = 20 THEN 'evening'
        END AS time_period,
        ABS(it.hour_of_day - tt.target_hour) AS time_distance,
        DENSE_RANK() OVER (
            PARTITION BY it.invoice_date_str, tt.target_hour
            ORDER BY ABS(it.hour_of_day - tt.target_hour)
        ) AS time_rank
    FROM invoice_times it
    CROSS JOIN target_times tt
)

    TO_TIMESTAMP(dc.invoice_date_str || ' ' ||
           LPAD(FLOOR(dc.target_hour)::text, 2, '0') || ':00:00',

    dc.invoice_date,
    dc.invoice_id,
    dc.time_period,
    dc.time_distance,
    EXTRACT(DAY FROM (dc.invoice_date - TO_TIMESTAMP(dc.invoice_date_str, 'YYYY-MM-DD'))) * 24 +
    EXTRACT(HOUR FROM (dc.invoice_date - TO_TIMESTAMP(dc.invoice_date_str, 'YYYY-MM-DD'))) +

   FROM my_table t) MATCH_RECOGNIZE(PARTITION BY cto
                                      ORDER BY rn MEASURES MATCH_NUMBER() AS mn, SUM(filesize) AS total_size ALL ROWS PER MATCH PATTERN ((same_nif* nif)* same_nif* end_nif) DEFINE same_nif AS nif = NEXT(nif), nif AS (NEXT(nif) IS NULL
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     OR nif != NEXT(nif))
                                      AND SUM(filesize) + NEXT(nif_size) <= 10, end_nif AS SUM(filesize) <= 10) MATCH_RECOGNIZE(PARTITION BY cto
                                                                                                                                      ORDER BY rn MEASURES MATCH_NUMBER() AS partition, FIRST(mn) AS first_mn ALL ROWS PER MATCH PATTERN ((same_nif* nif)+) DEFINE same_nif AS nif = NEXT(nif), nif AS (NEXT(nif) IS NULL
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    OR nif != NEXT(nif))
                                                                                                                                      AND mn - FIRST(mn) < 7)

WITH my_table AS (
    SELECT 'A' AS cto, 1 AS nif, 'A1' AS file_, 5 AS filesize
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'A' AS cto, 1 AS nif, 'A2' AS file_, 3 AS filesize
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'A' AS cto, 2 AS nif, 'A3' AS file_, 2 AS filesize
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'A' AS cto, 2 AS nif, 'A4' AS file_, 1 AS filesize
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'B' AS cto, 1 AS nif, 'B1' AS file_, 4 AS filesize
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'B' AS cto, 1 AS nif, 'B2' AS file_, 6 AS filesize
),
ranked_data AS (
    SELECT
        t.*,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY cto ORDER BY SUBSTRING(file_, 1, 1), CAST(SUBSTRING(file_, 2) AS INTEGER)) AS rn,
        SUM(filesize) OVER (PARTITION BY nif) AS nif_size
    FROM my_table t
),
with_lag AS (
    SELECT
        rd.*,
        LAG(rd.nif, 1, rd.nif) OVER (PARTITION BY rd.cto ORDER BY rd.rn) AS prev_nif
    FROM ranked_data rd
),
partition_groups AS (
    SELECT
        wl.*,
        SUM(CASE WHEN wl.nif != wl.prev_nif THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
            OVER (PARTITION BY wl.cto ORDER BY wl.rn) AS nif_group,
        SUM(wl.filesize) OVER (PARTITION BY wl.cto ORDER BY wl.rn) AS running_total
    FROM with_lag wl
),
group_totals AS (
    SELECT
        pg.*,
        SUM(pg.filesize) OVER (PARTITION BY pg.cto, pg.nif_group ORDER BY pg.rn ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS group_running_total
    FROM partition_groups pg
),
partition_boundaries AS (
    SELECT
        gt.*,
        LEAD(gt.nif_size, 1, 0) OVER (PARTITION BY gt.cto ORDER BY gt.rn) AS next_nif_size,
        CASE
            WHEN LEAD(gt.nif_size, 1, 0) OVER (PARTITION BY gt.cto ORDER BY gt.rn) +
                 (gt.running_total - gt.group_running_total) <= 10
            THEN 0
            ELSE 1
        END AS new_partition
    FROM group_totals gt
),
partitions_with_sum AS (
    SELECT
        pb.*,
        SUM(pb.new_partition) OVER (PARTITION BY pb.cto ORDER BY pb.rn) AS partition
    FROM partition_boundaries pb
),
partitions AS (
    SELECT
        pws.*,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY pws.cto, pws.partition ORDER BY pws.rn) AS subpartition,
        SUM(pws.filesize) OVER (PARTITION BY pws.cto, pws.partition) AS total_size
    FROM partitions_with_sum pws
)
SELECT
    cto,
    nif,
    file_,
    partition + 1 AS partition,
    subpartition AS subpartition,
    total_size
FROM partitions
WHERE partition < 7
ORDER BY cto, rn

It seems I have some duplicate entries in this table where the login name and person's name are identical, but they have different unique identifiers (`guid`).

I'm trying to analyze employee records based on their employee_id. My goal is to find all records that belong to a sequence of *three or more consecutive* employee IDs.

I'm having trouble identifying only those records that are part of a consecutive run of at least three based on their employee_id. For instance, if IDs 5, 6, 7, and 8 form a consecutive sequence, I'd want all four returned because they form a consecutive sequence of 3 or more. However, an employee record with an ID like 10, which isn't part of a consecutive block of at least three such records (e.g., IDs 9 or 11 don't exist or are not included), should be excluded.

How can I structure a query in PostgreSQL to select only those employee records that are part of a group of at least three records with consecutive IDs?
issue_sql: SELECT employee_id, last_name, first_name, CASE WHEN employee_id > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS emp_flag, SUM(CASE WHEN employee_id > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) OVER (ORDER BY employee_id NULLS FIRST) AS grp, employee_id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY employee_id NULLS FIRST) AS diff, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY CASE WHEN employee_id > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END ORDER BY hire_date NULLS FIRST) AS sal_rn, employee_id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY CASE WHEN employee_id > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END ORDER BY hire_date NULLS FIRST) AS sal_grp FROM employee
sol_sql: WITH temp AS (SELECT b.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY employee_id NULLS FIRST) - employee_id AS grp FROM employee AS b), temp2 AS (SELECT a.*, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY grp) AS cnt FROM temp AS a) SELECT employee_id, last_name, first_name FROM temp2 WHERE cnt >= 3 ORDER BY employee_id NULLS FIRST

WITH member_data AS (
    SELECT
        member_id,
        member_name,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY member_name) AS rn
    FROM "member_trunc"
),
tokenized_members AS (
    SELECT
        a."link_to_event",
        generate_series(1, length(a."link_to_member") - length(replace(a."link_to_member", '|', '')) + 1) AS position,
        split_part(a."link_to_member", '|', generate_series(1, length(a."link_to_member") - length(replace(a."link_to_member", '|', '')) + 1)) AS member_token
    FROM "attendance_trunc" a
    WHERE a."link_to_member" IS NOT NULL
),
member_names AS (
    SELECT
        tm."link_to_event",
        tm.position,
        COALESCE(md.member_name, 'Unknown Member') AS member_name
    FROM tokenized_members tm
    LEFT JOIN member_data md ON (tm.member_token = md.member_id AND md.rn = 1)
)
SELECT
    mn."link_to_event",
    string_agg(mn.member_name, '|' ORDER BY CASE
                    WHEN mn.position IS NULL THEN 9999
                    ELSE mn.position
                 END) AS replaced_members
FROM member_names mn
GROUP BY mn."link_to_event"
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT mn.position) > 0
ORDER BY mn."link_to_event"

        SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER () AS position,
               elem AS value
        FROM unnest(string_to_array(a."link_to_member", '|')) AS elem
    ) v
    INNER JOIN "member_trunc" m

) tmp

I have a table in PostgreSQL where category headers (like 'Rock') and the items belonging to them (like 'Track 1', 'Track 2') are stored sequentially, ordered by an ID. There isn't a direct link between an item and its header, only the order they appear in based on the ID. I need to create output that shows each item prefixed by its correct category header, for example, 'Rock: Track 1', 'Rock: Track 2', and then later 'Jazz: Track 3' if 'Jazz' appears after 'Track 2' but before 'Track 3'.

I've tried approaches based on ordering by the ID to find the relevant category for each item, but I'm running into trouble. Instead of each item getting linked to the *most recent* category header that appeared before it, my attempts seem to incorrectly group items, maybe associating many items with the very first category header encountered or something similar. It's not correctly identifying the *nearest preceding* category for each specific item.

How can I structure a query in PostgreSQL to correctly find the name of the category header record that immediately precedes each item record based on their sequential IDs?
issue_sql:
SELECT genre.name || ': ' || track.name AS grouped_tracks
FROM (
    SELECT
        MAX(CASE WHEN genre.name LIKE '%' THEN genre.name END)
        OVER (ORDER BY track.track_id) AS header,
        track.track_id,
        track.name, genre.name
    FROM track JOIN genre ON track.genre_id = genre.genre_id
) AS subquery
WHERE name NOT LIKE '%'
sol_sql:
WITH genre_with_headers AS (
    SELECT
        g.*,
        LAG(CASE WHEN g.name LIKE '%' THEN g.name END)
        OVER (ORDER BY g.genre_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS header
    FROM genre g
    WHERE g.name LIKE '%'
),
all_tracks AS (
    SELECT
        t.*,
        (SELECT ch.name
         FROM genre ch
         WHERE ch.genre_id < t.genre_id
         ORDER BY ch.genre_id DESC
         LIMIT 1) AS header
    FROM track t JOIN genre ON t.genre_id = genre.genre_id
    WHERE t.name NOT LIKE '%'
)
SELECT header || ': ' || name AS grouped_tracks
FROM all_tracks
ORDER BY track_id

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION FIND_CUSTOMER_COLUMN(
    IN_FIRST_NAME VARCHAR,
    IN_LAST_NAME VARCHAR,
    IN_COMPANY VARCHAR,
    IN_ADDRESS VARCHAR,
    IN_REQUESTED_COLUMN VARCHAR
) RETURNS VARCHAR AS $$
DECLARE
    result VARCHAR(255);
BEGIN
    SELECT
        CASE IN_REQUESTED_COLUMN
            WHEN 'FIRST_NAME' THEN first_name
            WHEN 'LAST_NAME' THEN last_name
            WHEN 'COMPANY' THEN company
            ELSE NULL
        END
    INTO result
    FROM customer
    WHERE first_name = IN_FIRST_NAME
      AND last_name = IN_LAST_NAME
      AND company = IN_COMPANY
      AND (IN_ADDRESS IS NULL OR address = IN_ADDRESS)
    LIMIT 1;

    RETURN result;
END;

I'm working with invoice data and need help categorizing invoices for each customer. My goal is to label each invoice as either 'New' or 'Followup'.

The logic should be: the very first invoice recorded for any given customer is always considered 'New'. Subsequent invoices for that same customer should be labeled 'Followup' but only if they occur within 30 days of the *immediately preceding* invoice for that customer. If more than 30 days pass between two consecutive invoices for an account, the later invoice should be marked as 'New', effectively restarting the sequence.

I've tried comparing invoice dates against the earliest invoice date for each customer, but this doesn't capture the rolling 30-day window correctly. It fails to identify 'Followup' invoices properly when multiple occur close together, and it doesn't reset to 'New' after a gap longer than 30 days.

I'm finding it tricky to set up the comparison between an invoice and the one right before it for the same customer. How can I structure a query in PostgreSQL to correctly apply this 'New'/'Followup' logic based on the 30-day gap from the *previous* invoice within each customer?

I've tried joining the relevant information together. However, figuring out how to reliably get only the *last* invoice ID, while correctly handling customers who might not have any invoices or have multiple invoices, is proving difficult. My attempts seem to either miss some customers, show incorrect invoice IDs, or sometimes list customers more than once.

How can I structure a query in PostgreSQL to get a distinct list of all customers with their first name, last name, a 'Yes'/'No' flag for being born between 1948 and 1960, and the single, most recent invoice ID (or handle cases where they have no invoices)?
issue_sql:
WITH CustomerInvoiceSummary AS (
    SELECT
        cu.customer_id,
        cu.first_name,
        cu.last_name,
        i.invoice_id,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY cu.customer_id ORDER BY i.invoice_id DESC NULLS LAST) AS invoice_rank
    FROM
        customer AS cu
    LEFT JOIN
        invoice AS i ON i.customer_id = cu.customer_id
),
BabyBoomerFlag AS (
    SELECT
        customer_id,
        first_name,
        last_name,
        CASE
            WHEN EXTRACT(YEAR FROM birth_date) BETWEEN 1948 AND 1960 THEN 'Yes'
            ELSE 'No'
        END AS is_baby_boomer
    FROM
        employee
)
SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.first_name,
    c.last_name,
    COALESCE(b.is_baby_boomer, 'No') AS age_old,
    CASE
        WHEN c.invoice_id IS NOT NULL THEN c.invoice_id
        ELSE NULL
    END AS last_invoice
FROM
    customerinvoicesummary AS c
LEFT JOIN
    babyboomerflag AS b ON b.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE
    c.invoice_rank = 1 OR c.invoice_rank IS NULL
GROUP BY
    c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name, b.is_baby_boomer, c.invoice_id
HAVING
    COUNT(c.invoice_id) <= 1
ORDER BY
    c.customer_id NULLS FIRST

issue_sql:
SELECT track_id FROM ( SELECT CASE WHEN media_type_id = 1 AND lead(media_type_id) OVER
(ORDER BY track_id) = 2 THEN REPLACE(CONCAT(track_id, lead(track_id) OVER (ORDER BY track_id)), ' ', '')

WHEN media_type_id = 1 AND lead(media_type_id) OVER (ORDER BY track_id) IS NULL THEN track_id, ROW_NUMBER()

sol_sql: WITH TrackSequence AS (SELECT t.track_id, t.media_type_id, t.name, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY t.media_type_id ORDER BY t.track_id NULLS FIRST) AS seq_num FROM track AS t WHERE t.media_type_id = 1), MediaTypeSequence AS (SELECT mt.media_type_id, mt.name, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY mt.media_type_id ORDER BY mt.media_type_id NULLS FIRST) AS seq_num FROM media_type AS mt WHERE mt.media_type_id = 1) SELECT a.track_id, a.name, b.media_type_id, b.name FROM tracksequence AS a LEFT JOIN mediatypesequence AS b ON a.media_type_id = b.media_type_id AND a.seq_num = b.seq_num ORDER BY a.seq_num NULLS FIRST

I'm working with some time-series data for movies in PostgreSQL. Each movie has multiple view records over time, identified by an ID and a date. One specific metric (let's call it 'hours_viewed') is sometimes missing (NULL) in these records.

My goal is to create a view or query result where, for each movie, any missing 'hours_viewed' value is replaced by the most recent *non-missing* 'hours_viewed' value recorded for that same movie up to that point in time. The results should still be ordered chronologically for each movie, showing the original date and ID alongside the potentially filled-in 'hours_viewed' value.

I've tried using window functions to look back at previous rows for the same movie, ordered by date, but I'm running into an issue. It seems more complex than simply looking at the immediately previous row, especially if there are several consecutive missing values before a valid one appears.

How can I structure a query in PostgreSQL to achieve this? I need to effectively carry forward the last observed non-null 'hours_viewed' value for each movie to fill in any subsequent nulls, maintaining the original date order for all records.

    SELECT
        t.track_id,

I'm working with a dataset containing customer information, including their country. I need to generate a single string that summarizes customer countries based on their uniqueness.

My goal is to check if all the customers are from the same country. If there's only one unique country present across all customers (ignoring any missing countries), I want the output to be just that single country value. However, if there are multiple different countries, I want the output to be a string showing the range, formatted like 'lowest_country-highest_country'.

I've tried using conditional logic to check the number of unique countries and then applying different formatting based on the result. I've also looked into ways to find the minimum and maximum country values when there are multiple countries. However, I'm running into issues getting the final string formatted correctly, especially when combining the minimum and maximum values with the hyphen, and I suspect it might be related to how I'm handling the country values which might not always be text.

How can I construct a query that correctly identifies whether there is one unique country or multiple, and then outputs either the single country or the 'min-max' range as a properly formatted string?
issue_sql: WITH CustomerGroups AS (SELECT CASE WHEN state IS NULL THEN 'Unknown' ELSE state END AS customer_group, country FROM customer WHERE NOT country IS NULL), GroupedCountries AS (SELECT customer_group, MIN(country) AS min_country, MAX(country) AS max_country, COUNT(DISTINCT country) AS distinct_country_count FROM customergroups GROUP BY customer_group) SELECT customer_group, CASE WHEN distinct_country_count > 1 THEN MIN(min_country)     || '-' || MAX(max_country) ELSE MAX(max_country)   END AS concat_countries FROM groupedcountries GROUP BY customer_group, distinct_country_count ORDER BY customer_group NULLS FIRST
sol_sql: SELECT CASE WHEN COUNT(DISTINCT country) = 1 THEN MAX(CAST(country AS VARCHAR(50))) ELSE CONCAT(CAST(MIN(country) AS VARCHAR(50)), '-', CAST(MAX(country) AS VARCHAR(50))) END AS concat_countries FROM customer WHERE NOT country IS NULL

My goal is to produce a result that lists each employee's first name, the title, and the difference between the identifier for their 'Senior Engineer' title and the identifier for their 'Staff' title. So, for a given employee, I want to subtract the 'Staff' ID from the 'Senior Engineer' ID.

I've tried structuring this in a few ways, attempting to isolate the 'Senior Engineer' ID and the 'Staff' ID for each employee before calculating the difference. However, my attempts feel overly complicated and I'm not quite getting the result I need, especially when trying to bring the two relevant identifiers together on one line for the calculation. It seems difficult to access both values simultaneously for the subtraction.

issue_sql:
WITH EmployeeTitles AS (
    SELECT e.first_name AS employee_name, t.title, e.id, t.employee_id,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY e.id, t.title ORDER BY CASE WHEN t.title = 'Senior Engineer' THEN 0 ELSE 1 END NULLS FIRST) AS status_priority
    FROM employee AS e
    LEFT JOIN title AS t ON e.id = t.employee_id
    WHERE t.title IN ('Senior Engineer', 'Staff')
),
TitleStats AS (
    SELECT employee_name, title,
    MAX(CASE WHEN title = 'Senior Engineer' THEN employee_id END) AS legal_id,
    MAX(CASE WHEN title = 'Staff' THEN employee_id END) AS banned_id
    FROM EmployeeTitles
    GROUP BY employee_name, title
)
SELECT et.employee_name, et.title, ts.legal_id, ts.banned_id,
CASE WHEN et.title = 'Senior Engineer' AND et.status_priority = 1 THEN ts.legal_id - ts.banned_id END AS id_diff
FROM EmployeeTitles AS et
JOIN TitleStats AS ts ON et.employee_name = ts.employee_name AND et.title = ts.title
WHERE et.title IN ('Senior Engineer', 'Staff')
ORDER BY et.employee_name ASC NULLS FIRST, et.title ASC NULLS FIRST

I'm working with data that links album identifiers to their constituent track names. Each album can have several associated track names listed in separate records. My goal is to transform this data so that for each album identifier, I get a single row showing its first three track names in distinct columns, let's call them `track1`, `track2`, and `track3`. The order of track names matters, based on their original identifiers.

To achieve this, I first tried assigning a sequence number to each track name within its album group. Then, I attempted to use this sequenced information, potentially combining it back with the track name data, to pivot these track names into the desired columnar format.

However, this approach isn't working as expected. Instead of getting one row per album, I'm seeing a huge number of rows, with album identifiers repeated many times and seemingly incorrect combinations of track names appearing across the columns. It feels like some kind of unintended cross-joining or duplication is happening.

Ideally, the output should look something like this: one row for each album ID, with the first track name under `track1`, the second under `track2`, and the third under `track3`. If a album has fewer than three track names, the corresponding columns should just be empty or null.

How can I structure my query correctly in PostgreSQL to get this pivoted view of the first three track names per album without generating all these extra, incorrect rows?
issue_sql: WITH trackrns AS (SELECT album_id, name, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY album_id ORDER BY track_id NULLS FIRST) AS RN FROM track) SELECT album_id, MAX(CASE WHEN RN = 1 THEN name END) AS track1, MAX(CASE WHEN RN = 2 THEN name END) AS track2, MAX(CASE WHEN RN = 3 THEN name END) AS track3 FROM trackrns JOIN track ON trackrns.album_id = track.album_id GROUP BY album_id

For instance, if the sequence is Show A, Show B, Show C, Show D, Show E, Show F..., I'd want to see pairs like (Show A, Show E), (Show B, Show F), etc.

I've been trying different ways to achieve this, involving ranking the tv shows using various attributes and even grouping them first, but it feels like I'm making it much more complicated than it needs to be. Once I've identified these movies or TV shows (the ones with variety in their duration types), I then need to find out, for each one, which of its duration types comes first alphabetically. So, if a movie had types 'ANNUALLY', 'MONTHLY', and 'SEMI_ANNUALLY', I'd want to identify it as having multiple types, and then retrieve just the 'ANNUALLY' type for it.

I've been trying different ways to structure a query for this, but I'm finding it tricky to both check for the presence of multiple distinct duration types per movie/TV show and then select the alphabetically earliest type just for those movies/TV shows. issue_sql: WITH BondTypeRanking AS (SELECT id, movie_id, duration, CASE WHEN duration = '-' THEN 1 WHEN duration = '=' THEN 2 WHEN duration = '#' THEN 3 ELSE CAST(duration AS INT)   END AS bond_type_rank FROM view_summary), MoleculeWithMultipleBondTypes AS (SELECT movie_id FROM view_summary GROUP BY movie_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN duration = '-' THEN 'single' WHEN duration = '=' THEN 'double' WHEN duration = '#' THEN 'triple' ELSE duration END) > 1) SELECT b.movie_id, b.duration FROM (SELECT btr.movie_id, btr.duration, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY btr.movie_id ORDER BY btr.bond_type_rank NULLS FIRST, LENGTH(CAST(btr.duration AS TEXT)) NULLS FIRST  , btr.duration NULLS FIRST) AS rn FROM bondtyperanking AS btr INNER JOIN moleculewithmultiplebondtypes AS m ON btr.movie_id = m.movie_id WHERE NOT btr.bond_type_rank IS NULL  ) AS b WHERE b.rn = 1 ORDER BY CASE WHEN b.movie_id LIKE 'TR%' THEN 0 ELSE 1 END NULLS FIRST  , b.movie_id NULLS FIRST

SELECT

    (
        SELECT
            CAST(i.invoice_id AS TEXT) AS invoice_id
        FROM invoice i
        WHERE i.customer_id = c.customer_id

    j1.value->>'nvarchar_column' AS nvarchar_column

    {"id_column": 1234, "decimal_column": 12.34, "nvarchar_column": "asdf"},
    {"id_column": 5678, "decimal_column": 56.78, "nvarchar_column": "fdsa"}
  ]'::json) WITH ORDINALITY AS j1(value, key)
)
SELECT
  key,
  id_column,
  decimal_column,
  nvarchar_column,
  value->>'nvarchar_column' AS "another example"
FROM json_data

How can I get the final list of artists and their scores, ordered properly by the total combined score they received from all the keywords?

WITH KEYWORDMATCHES AS
  (SELECT A.artist_id AS ID,
          CASE
              WHEN POSITION(LOWER('AC/DC') IN LOWER(A.name)) > 0 THEN 'AC/DC'

          CASE
              WHEN POSITION(LOWER('Accept') IN LOWER(A.name)) > 0 THEN 'Accept'
          END AS COLBKEYWORD,
          CASE
              WHEN POSITION(LOWER('Aerosmith') IN LOWER(A.name)) > 0 THEN 'Aerosmith'
          END AS COLCKEYWORD
   FROM ARTIST AS A),
     KEYWORDSCORES AS
  (SELECT ID,
          STRING_AGG(COLAKEYWORD, ', ') FILTER (WHERE COLAKEYWORD IS NOT NULL) AS KEYWORDSA,
          STRING_AGG(COLBKEYWORD, ', ') FILTER (WHERE COLBKEYWORD IS NOT NULL) AS KEYWORDSB,

             OR LAG(t.name) OVER (PARTITION BY t.track_id ORDER BY t.track_id) <> t.name

How can I accurately determine the correct week number for each period's start date and combine it with the year to produce the 'YYYY.WW' formatted string, ensuring the week number is always zero-padded to two digits?

        vs.id AS ViewSummary_ID,
        COALESCE(tv.id, m.id) AS Item_ID

    LEFT JOIN distinctCombos dc ON dc.ViewSummary_ID = vs.id
    GROUP BY vs.id
)
SELECT
    COUNT(DISTINCT itemList) AS UniqueGroups
FROM itemComboCount

I'm working with two sets of date ranges. One set defines when employees are generally considered active, with a start and end date for each active spell. The other set defines blackout periods, again with start and end dates, during which employees are temporarily restricted.

My goal is to identify the precise time intervals where employees were *both* active *and* not under any blackout restrictions. The challenge comes when blackout periods overlap with each other or span across parts of the active periods. I need to effectively 'subtract' the total duration covered by *any* blackout from the active periods.

I've attempted to figure this out by looking at how the ranges overlap, maybe trying to combine the blackout periods first, but I'm struggling to get the logic right to isolate only those times that are active but completely clear of *any* blackout. It feels like I'm overcomplicating it, and the results aren't matching what I expect.

How can I effectively calculate these final 'clear' operational time ranges in PostgreSQL, correctly handling the potential for overlapping blackout periods?

        spell_starts AS (
            SELECT start_date, end_date
            FROM blackout_periods s1
            WHERE NOT EXISTS (
                SELECT 1
                FROM blackout_periods s2
                WHERE s2.start_date < s1.start_date
                AND s1.start_date <= s2.end_date
            )
        ),
        spell_ends AS (
            SELECT start_date, end_date
            FROM blackout_periods t1
            WHERE NOT EXISTS (
                SELECT 1
                FROM blackout_periods t2
                WHERE t2.start_date <= t1.end_date
                AND t1.end_date < t2.end_date
            )
        )
        SELECT s.start_date, MIN(e.end_date) as end_date
        FROM spell_starts s
        INNER JOIN spell_ends e
        ON s.start_date <= e.end_date
        GROUP BY s.start_date;

        FROM (
            SELECT (end_date + INTERVAL '1 day') AS start_date
                ,LEAD((start_date - INTERVAL '1 day'), 1, '9999-01-01'::date) OVER (ORDER BY start_date) AS end_date
            FROM merge_table_2

            UNION ALL


            SELECT '1900-01-01'::date AS start_date
                ,(MIN(start_date) - INTERVAL '1 day') AS end_date
            FROM merge_table_2
        ) k
        WHERE start_date <= end_date
        AND '1900-01-01'::date <= start_date
        AND end_date <= '9999-01-01'::date;

SELECT CASE WHEN t1.start_date < t2.start_date THEN t2.start_date ELSE t1.start_date END AS start_date
            ,CASE WHEN t1.end_date < t2.end_date THEN t1.end_date ELSE t2.end_date END AS end_date

WITH cte AS (
    SELECT t FROM (
        SELECT start_date AS t FROM account_activity
        UNION ALL
        SELECT end_date FROM account_activity
        UNION ALL
        SELECT start_date - INTERVAL '1 DAY' FROM blackout_periods
        UNION ALL
        SELECT end_date + INTERVAL '1 DAY' FROM blackout_periods
    ) AS a
),
cte2 AS (
    SELECT t AS s, COALESCE(LEAD(t, 1) OVER (ORDER BY t NULLS FIRST), t) AS e
    FROM cte AS a
)
SELECT s, e
FROM cte2 AS a
WHERE NOT EXISTS(
    SELECT 1
    FROM blackout_periods AS b
    WHERE s BETWEEN start_date - INTERVAL '1 DAY' AND end_date + INTERVAL '1 DAY'
    AND e BETWEEN start_date - INTERVAL '1 DAY' AND end_date + INTERVAL '1 DAY'
)
AND EXISTS(
    SELECT 1
    FROM account_activity AS b
    WHERE s BETWEEN start_date AND end_date
    AND e BETWEEN start_date AND end_date
)

Here's my SQL:

```sql

    part_num,
    name as original_name,

FROM parts
WHERE name ~ '\s+$';

WHERE name ~ '\s+$';

The regex pattern works fine when I test it on other tables. I'm confused because the database definitely exists and contains the data I need to clean up.

What am I missing here? Why can't PostgreSQL find these tables?

I'm trying to clean up trailing whitespace from names in my `person` table and city names in my `city` table in a PostgreSQL database. The person table cleanup works fine, but I'm having issues with the city table update that needs to handle various Unicode whitespace characters.

Here's my SQL:

```sql
SELECT 
    id,
    full_name AS original_name,
    regexp_replace(full_name, '\s+$', '') AS trimmed_name,
    length(full_name) AS original_length,
    length(regexp_replace(full_name, '\s+$', '')) AS trimmed_length
FROM person
WHERE full_name ~ '\s+$';
UPDATE person
SET full_name = regexp_replace(full_name, '\s+$', '')
WHERE full_name ~ '\s+$';
UPDATE city
SET city_name = regexp_replace(city_name, '[\s\u00A0\u180E\u2007\u200B\u200C\u200D\u202F\u2060\uFEFF]+$', '')
WHERE city_name ~ '[\s' + '\u00A0\u180E\u2007\u200B\u200C\u200D\u202F\u2060\uFEFF]+$';
```

The first two statements execute successfully, but when I run this script, I'm getting an error on the third UPDATE statement: `ERROR: operator does not exist: text + unknown`. I thought I could build the regex pattern by concatenating strings in the WHERE clause to make it more readable, but PostgreSQL seems to be complaining about the `+` operator. The regexp_replace in the SET clause works fine with the full pattern, so I'm confused why the WHERE clause is failing. What's the correct way to handle this regex pattern in the WHERE clause?

```sql

    id,
    full_name AS original_name,
    regexp_replace(full_name, '\s+$', '') AS trimmed_name,
    length(full_name) AS original_length,
    length(regexp_replace(full_name, '\s+$', '')) AS trimmed_length
FROM person
WHERE regexp_replace(full_name, '\s+$', '') != full_name;
UPDATE person
SET full_name = regexp_replace(full_name, '\s+$', '')
WHERE full_name ~ '\s+$';

SET city_name = regexp_replace(city_name, '[\s\u00A0\u180E\u2007\u200B\u200C\u200D\u202F\u2060\uFEFF]+$', '')

The UPDATE statements run much faster in comparison. I know there are only a few thousand rows with trailing spaces, so I feel like this should be much quicker. Is there a more efficient way to write the WHERE clause in my SELECT statement to avoid this performance issue?

```sql

    actor_id,
    first_name,
    last_name,
    regexp_replace(first_name, '\s+$', '') AS first_name_trimmed,
    regexp_replace(last_name, '\s+$', '') AS last_name_trimmed
FROM actor
ORDER BY regexp_replace(first_name, '\s+$', ''), regexp_replace(last_name, '\s+$', '');
SELECT 
    address_id,
    address,
    regexp_replace(address, '\s+$', '') AS address_trimmed,
    district,
    regexp_replace(district, '\s+$', '') AS district_trimmed

ORDER BY regexp_replace(address, '\s+$', '');

    film_id,
    title,
    regexp_replace(title, '\s+$', '') AS title_trimmed,
    description,
    regexp_replace(description, '\s+$', '') AS description_trimmed

ORDER BY regexp_replace(description, '\s+$', '');
UPDATE actor 
SET first_name = regexp_replace(first_name, '\s+$', ''),
    last_name = regexp_replace(last_name, '\s+$', '');
```

The actor table has about 500K rows, address has 1M rows, and film has 2M rows. Each SELECT query is taking 10-15 seconds to complete, which seems way too long for what should be a simple operation. I'm trying to create a function that finds employees with upcoming birthdays within a specified date range. The function should use `current_date` by default but allow passing a custom reference date for testing purposes.

Here's my SQL:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION f_mmdd(date)
RETURNS integer
LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE AS
'SELECT to_char($1, ''MMDD'')::integer';
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS employee_mmdd_birth_date_idx ON employee(f_mmdd(birth_date::date));
WITH date_range AS (
    SELECT generate_series(0, 13) AS d
),
target_dates AS (
    SELECT f_mmdd((current_date + d)::date) AS mmdd
    FROM date_range
)
SELECT 
    e.employee_id,
    e.first_name,
    e.last_name,
    e.birth_date,
    e.title
FROM employee e
WHERE f_mmdd(e.birth_date::date) IN (SELECT mmdd FROM target_dates)
ORDER BY f_mmdd(e.birth_date::date);
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION f_upcoming_birthdays(_reference_date date DEFAULT current_date, _days int DEFAULT 14)
RETURNS TABLE(employee_id integer, first_name character varying, last_name character varying, birth_date timestamp, title character varying)
LANGUAGE sql VOLATILE AS
$$
    WITH date_range AS (
        SELECT generate_series(0, _days - 1) AS d
    ),
    target_dates AS (
        SELECT to_char((_reference_date + d)::date, 'MMDD')::integer AS mmdd
        FROM date_range
    )
    SELECT 
        e.employee_id,
        e.first_name,
        e.last_name,
        e.birth_date,
        e.title
    FROM employee e
    WHERE to_char(e.birth_date::date, 'MMDD')::integer IN (SELECT mmdd FROM target_dates)
    ORDER BY to_char(e.birth_date::date, 'MMDD')::integer
$$;
SELECT * FROM f_upcoming_birthdays();
SELECT * FROM f_upcoming_birthdays(date '2024-12-25', 7);
```

The function works correctly and returns the right results, but the performance is terrible. When I run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, I see it's doing a sequential scan on the employee table even though I created a functional index on `f_mmdd(birth_date::date)`. The standalone query before the function definition uses the index just fine, but when wrapped in the function, PostgreSQL ignores the index completely. I marked the function as `VOLATILE` since it uses `current_date` by default, but now I'm wondering if that's causing the planner to avoid optimizations. Why isn't my functional index being used inside the function, and how can I fix this performance issue?

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS citext WITH SCHEMA public;

-- Create a function to convert text arrays to lowercase (for case-insensitive IN operations)
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION lower(t text[]) RETURNS text[]
LANGUAGE SQL IMMUTABLE
AS $$
    SELECT lower($1::text)::text[]
$$;

-- Example query: Find customers with specific email addresses (case-insensitive)
SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name, email
FROM customer
WHERE lower(email) = ANY(lower(ARRAY['ronald.weiner@sakilacustomer.org', 'LUCILLE.HOLMES@sakilacustomer.org', 'kay.caldwell@sakilacustomer.org']));

-- Alternative approach: Find actors by last name (case-insensitive)
SELECT actor_id, first_name, last_name
FROM actor
WHERE lower(last_name) = ANY(lower(ARRAY['AKROYD', 'bridges', 'HuNt']));

-- Create a case-insensitive index on customer email for better performance
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS ix_customer_email_lower ON customer(lower(email));

        1917 AS the_year,

I'm trying to analyze daily flight counts and passenger counts over rolling 30-day windows in a PostgreSQL airline database. I need to calculate the ratio of daily values to their respective 30-day totals for both flights and passengers.

Here's my query:

```sql
WITH daily_flights AS (
    SELECT 
        actual_departure::date AS flight_date,
        COUNT(DISTINCT flight_id) AS daily_count
    FROM flights
    WHERE actual_departure IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY actual_departure::date
)
SELECT 
    flight_date,
    daily_count,
    SUM(daily_count) OVER (ORDER BY flight_date ROWS BETWEEN 29 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS monthly_count,
    ROUND(100.0 * daily_count / NULLIF(SUM(daily_count) OVER (ORDER BY flight_date ROWS BETWEEN 29 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 0), 2) AS daily_to_monthly_ratio
FROM daily_flights
ORDER BY flight_date;
WITH daily_passengers AS (
    SELECT 
        f.actual_departure AS flight_date,
        COUNT(DISTINCT t.passenger_id) AS daily_passengers
    FROM flights f
    JOIN ticket_flights tf ON f.flight_id = tf.flight_id
    JOIN tickets t ON tf.ticket_no = t.ticket_no
    WHERE f.actual_departure IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY f.actual_departure
)
SELECT 
    flight_date,
    daily_passengers,
    SUM(daily_passengers) OVER (ORDER BY flight_date ROWS BETWEEN 29 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS monthly_passengers,
    ROUND(100.0 * daily_passengers / NULLIF(SUM(daily_passengers) OVER (ORDER BY flight_date ROWS BETWEEN 29 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 0), 2) AS engagement_ratio
FROM daily_passengers
ORDER BY flight_date;
```

I'm trying to count distinct users who left reviews over a rolling 3-year window for each year from 2008 to 2014 in my PostgreSQL database. The idea is that for each year, I want to count users who joined the platform within that year and the two preceding years.

Here's my query:

```sql
-- Count distinct users who left reviews for each business over a rolling 3-year window
SELECT y.actual_year,
       (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT r.user_id)
        FROM Reviews r
        JOIN Users u ON r.user_id = u.user_id
        WHERE u.user_yelping_since_year BETWEEN y.actual_year - 2 AND y.actual_year
       ) AS distinct_users
FROM Years y
WHERE y.actual_year BETWEEN 2008 AND 2014
GROUP BY y.actual_year
ORDER BY y.actual_year;
```

But I'm getting this error: `ERROR: relation "reviews" does not exist`. I've also tried alternative approaches using `generate_series` and `LEFT JOIN`, but they all give me similar "relation does not exist" errors for the tables I'm referencing. I can see these tables in my database when I list them with `\dt`, and I can query them individually in other contexts, so I know they exist. The error message is confusing because it says the relation doesn't exist, but I'm certain the tables are there in the `public_review_platform` database.

What am I missing here? Why is PostgreSQL saying these tables don't exist when they clearly do?

WITH medal_stats AS (
    SELECT 
        p.id,
        p.full_name,
        COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE m.medal_name = 'Gold') AS gold_count,
        COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE m.medal_name = 'Silver') AS silver_count,
        COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE m.medal_name = 'Bronze') AS bronze_count
    FROM person p
    JOIN games_competitor gc ON p.id = gc.person_id
    JOIN competitor_event ce ON gc.id = ce.competitor_id
    JOIN medal m ON ce.medal_id = m.id
    WHERE m.medal_name IN ('Gold', 'Silver', 'Bronze')
    GROUP BY p.id, p.full_name
)

    full_name,
    gold_count,
    silver_count,
    bronze_count,
    gold_count + silver_count + bronze_count AS total_medals,
    gold_count * 3 + silver_count * 2 + bronze_count AS weighted_score
FROM medal_stats
WHERE gold_count + silver_count + bronze_count > 5
ORDER BY total_medals DESC, gold_count DESC
LIMIT 20;

        AVG(range) AS avg_range,
        STDDEV(range) AS stddev_range
    FROM aircrafts_data
)
SELECT 
    aircraft_code,
    range,
    (range - stats.avg_range) / NULLIF(stats.stddev_range, 0) AS range_zscore
FROM aircrafts_data
CROSS JOIN stats
ORDER BY aircraft_code;

WITH flight_stats AS (
    SELECT 
        AVG(amount) AS avg_amount,
        STDDEV(amount) AS stddev_amount
    FROM ticket_flights
),
booking_stats AS (
    SELECT 
        AVG(total_amount) AS avg_total,
        STDDEV(total_amount) AS stddev_total
    FROM public
)
SELECT 
    tf.ticket_no,
    tf.flight_id,
    tf.amount,
    (tf.amount - fs.avg_amount) / NULLIF(fs.stddev_amount, 0) AS amount_zscore,
    b.total_amount,
    (b.total_amount - bs.avg_total) / NULLIF(bs.stddev_total, 0) AS total_amount_zscore
FROM ticket_flights tf
JOIN tickets t ON tf.ticket_no = t.ticket_no
JOIN public b ON t.book_ref = b.book_ref
CROSS JOIN flight_stats fs
CROSS JOIN booking_stats bs
LIMIT 100;

        STDDEV(milliseconds) AS stddev_milliseconds,

        STDDEV(bytes) AS stddev_bytes,
        AVG(unit_price) AS avg_unit_price,

Here's my query:

```sql

The query works and returns the correct results, but it's incredibly slow — taking over 2 minutes to execute on a database with about 500k flight records and 1 million ticket records. Here's my SQL:

-- Calculate a future date by adding runtime (in minutes) as days to the release_date for movies
SELECT 
    title,
    release_date,
    runtime,
    release_date + runtime * INTERVAL "1" day AS projected_end_date
FROM movie
WHERE release_date IS NOT NULL 
  AND runtime IS NOT NULL;
-- Alternative using make_interval: Add runtime days to the created_date for seasons
SELECT 
    title,
    created_date,
    runtime,
    created_date + make_interval(days => runtime::integer) AS extended_date
FROM season
WHERE created_date IS NOT NULL

    m.title,
    vs.start_date,
    vs.cumulative_weeks_in_top10,

I'm trying to write a query that analyzes customer purchasing behavior in our bookstore database. I need to get customers who have placed more than one order, along with various aggregated metrics including how many of their orders used expensive shipping (cost > 10) and their average spending on long books (over 300 pages).

Here's my query:

```sql
SELECT 
    c.customer_id,
    c.first_name,
    c.last_name,
    COUNT(*) AS total_orders,
    COUNT(*) WHERE sm.cost > 10 AS expensive_shipping_orders,
    SUM(ol.price) AS total_spent,
    SUM(ol.price) FILTER (WHERE sm.cost > 10) AS spent_with_expensive_shipping,
    AVG(ol.price) FILTER (WHERE b.num_pages > 300) AS avg_price_long_books
FROM customer c
JOIN cust_order co ON c.customer_id = co.customer_id
JOIN order_line ol ON co.order_id = ol.order_id
JOIN book b ON ol.book_id = b.book_id
JOIN shipping_method sm ON co.shipping_method_id = sm.method_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name
